name: ERITREA

flag.title: Flag of Eritrea
flag.note: Green, red & blue with olive wreath

lead: Eritrea hugs Africa's north-east Red Sea coast. Its capital Asmara sits on a cool plateau over 2,300 m high, looking like an Italian village on Africa. Freed after a 30-year independence war in 1993, Eritrea packs ancient ruins, coral reefs, dugongs, and nine peoples into a land the size of England.
geo: Eritrea splits into three zones: a cool fertile highland plateau where most people live; a scorching coastal lowland strip along the Red Sea; and a flat dry western plain bordering Sudan. The highlands drop to the coast in just 60 km of hairpin roads.

The Red Sea coast stretches nearly 2,000 km and includes the Dahlak Archipelago — over 120 islands, most uninhabited, ringed by coral reefs. Inland, seasonal rivers rush after rain then vanish into sandy beds for months.
animals: Eritrea's Red Sea shelters some of the world's healthiest dugongs — gentle sea-cows grazing on seagrass meadows. Green and hawksbill turtles haul onto Dahlak beaches to lay eggs. Dolphins are so common that fishermen consider them neighbours.

Up on rocky highlands, Nubian ibex pick along clifftops with curved scimitar horns. Vervet monkeys raid gardens near Asmara, and forests hide bushbuck and leopard. Over 500 bird species have been recorded here.
culture: Eritrea has nine recognised ethnic groups, each with its own language and dress. The Tigrinya-speaking highlanders share a deep coffee ceremony: beans roasted in front of guests, ground by hand, and poured three times — refusing a cup is rude.

Injera — a big spongy flatbread made from teff grain — is plate, spoon, and food all at once, shared from one platter. Music blends African rhythms with the krar lyre, and colourful woven shawls are worn to every celebration.
history: Ancient Eritrea was part of the mighty Aksumite Empire and its Red Sea ports buzzed with merchants from Arabia, India, and Rome. The harbour city of Adulis was one of the ancient world's most important trading posts.

Italy colonised Eritrea in 1890, filling Asmara with Art Deco buildings. After WWII Eritrea was absorbed by Ethiopia. A 30-year armed struggle followed; in 1993 over 99% of Eritreans voted yes to independence.
wows: Asmara is Africa's first modernist UNESCO city — its streets look like a 1930s Italian film set.
In 1937 Eritrea had the world's longest cableway: 72 km of gondolas hauling cargo from sea to capital.
Eritrea's Red Sea corals survive water temperatures that would bleach reefs almost anywhere else on Earth.
Eritrea banned single-use plastic bags in 2005, one of the first countries in Africa to do so.
The country recognises nine official languages — more than most nations three times its size.
At least half of all Red Sea dugongs depend on Eritrea's and Sudan's seagrass beds to survive.
In 1993 Eritreans voted 99.83% for independence — one of the highest results ever recorded anywhere.

myths.fact: Eritrea has been fully independent since 1993, with its own government, currency, and flag, after a 30-year independence war and a UN-monitored vote.
The cool highlands above 2,000 m have good farmland and a pleasant climate; Asmara is famously mild and leafy, nicknamed 'the Rome of Africa'.
